projects.title: Enterprise HR Platform — Employee Management Module
projects.scope: Core employee records, org hierarchy, and role-based access.
projects.context: A mid-sized enterprise needed to digitize its HR operations across four interconnected Angular applications. On the Employee Management module, I was the sole front-end developer, owning the implementation while coordinating with backend developers, designers, and QA. This module holds the employee records and organizational structure the other HR modules read from.
projects.challenge: I carried the module's front-end implementation alone, so design and data-model questions came to me first. Employee data feeds every other HR app, so the data model, shared UI patterns, and permission rules had to be right at the start. Four apps with different business scopes had to share one set of forms, tables, and access rules.
solution: Implemented the module's employee and org-unit TypeScript interfaces against the platform's shared data model, so the contract stayed aligned across the four apps.
Built a recursive tree component for the organizational hierarchy on the shared UI library, with an API other feature modules could compose.
Implemented route guards and a structural directive that show or hide UI by role and permission, so access rules live in one place.
Built reusable form and table components for employee records and documented their conventions, so later contributors could extend the module.
Built a typed API service layer for employee endpoints, so components read data through one boundary and error handling stayed consistent.
role: Front-end owner for the Employee Management module: made implementation decisions and settled component and API contracts with backend and design.
Built the reusable form, table, and org-tree components used throughout the module.
Implemented the role-based access layer: route guards and the permission-based structural directive.
Wrote and maintained the API service layer for employee endpoints.
Reviewed module pull requests and kept structure and conventions consistent for other contributors.
outcome: Shipped the Employee Management module to production as part of a four-app enterprise HR platform.
Was the sole front-end developer on the module, owning its implementation inside the platform's established Angular architecture and shared component library.
Delivered the employee and org-unit data foundation the other three HR modules depend on.
lessons: I would define the permission model as a shared contract earlier, before building screens.
I would add visual regression tests for the shared components from the first sprint.

projects.title: Enterprise HR Platform — Attendance Management Module
projects.scope: Real-time attendance tracking and reporting dashboards.
projects.context: The same HR platform needed a way to track attendance across the organization and report on it. I was one of the front-end developers on this module, working alongside the other three apps on shared components and conventions.
projects.challenge: Attendance data changes constantly, and managers need fast, readable summaries. Large lists and frequent updates had to stay responsive.
solution: Attendance events flow through RxJS streams into a service-level store; views subscribe with the async pipe.
Used the platform's shared filter and date-range components across the module.
Dashboard widgets are small presentational components fed by one data stream.
role: Implemented the stream-based data layer for attendance records.
Optimized list rendering with OnPush change detection and trackBy.
Contributed shared filter components to the common library.
outcome: Shipped the Attendance Management module to production as part of the four-app HR platform.
Built the stream-based data layer and OnPush/trackBy rendering that kept large, frequently updating attendance lists responsive.
Reporting dashboards composed the platform's shared filter and date-range components.
lessons: I would agree on update frequency and data shape with the back end before building the stream layer.
I would add a shared loading and empty-state pattern sooner.

projects.title: Enterprise HR Platform — Training Management Module
projects.scope: Multi-step training workflows with clear progress states.
projects.context: HR teams needed to plan, assign and follow up on employee training. I was one of the front-end developers on this module, aligning with the platform on shared UI patterns and workflow conventions.
projects.challenge: Training requests move through several steps and states. Users need to know where an item stands and what to do next, so the state model and progress indicators have to be explicit.
solution: A reusable stepper workflow built on Angular Material, with per-step validation.
Workflow states modeled as TypeScript union types, so invalid states fail at compile time.
Used the platform's shared status badge and timeline components.
role: Built the multi-step forms and workflow screens.
Modeled workflow states and transitions in TypeScript.
Built status and progress components on top of the shared library.
outcome: Shipped the Training Management module to production as part of the four-app HR platform.
Modeled workflow states as TypeScript union types, so invalid transitions fail at compile time.
Kept the stepper and status components consistent with the shared library's API.
lessons: I would document the workflow state model in the repo for the next developer.
I would test each transition with unit tests earlier.

projects.title: Enterprise HR Platform — Workload Management Module
projects.context: Managers needed a clear view of team workload and available capacity. I was one of the front-end developers on this module, working within the platform's shared visualization and service patterns.
projects.challenge: Capacity data is dense, and managers need over- and under-allocation visible at a glance. Charts and derived metrics needed consistent APIs and rendering that stays fast on large datasets.
solution: Implemented chart and heat-map views through the platform's shared UI components, with one API across the module.
Computed derived values (utilization, remaining capacity) in services, so templates stayed thin.
Lazy-loaded the visualization code so it downloads when the module opens.
role: Implemented the services that calculate capacity and utilization.
Handled lazy loading and bundle-size checks for the module.
outcome: Shipped the Workload Management module to production as part of the four-app HR platform.
Implemented chart and heat-map views through the platform's shared UI components, keeping visualization consistent across modules.
Moved capacity calculations into services and lazy-loaded visualization code, keeping the module's initial bundle small.
lessons: I would set accessibility rules for charts (text alternatives, color contrast) at the start.
I would profile large datasets earlier to choose between SVG and canvas.

architecture.title: Shared component library
architecture.text: Tables, forms, dialogs, status badges and charts lived in one shared module with a stable API. Feature modules composed them instead of rebuilding them.

architecture.title: Service layer and API abstraction
architecture.text: Components reached the API through a typed ApiService rather than HttpClient directly. Feature services built on top of it.

architecture.title: RxJS state management
architecture.text: Services exposed observables. Components subscribed with the async pipe, so subscriptions cleaned themselves up and state flowed one way.

architecture.title: Lazy loading and module structure
architecture.text: Code was split into core, shared and feature areas. Each feature was lazy-loaded by route, so users downloaded only what they opened.
